paragraphs: Learning across changing domains becomes harder when classes appear at very different frequencies. Within a domain, scarce classes can remain poorly learned. Across domains, the frequency pattern can change, creating a second problem: a model must retain knowledge of previously common classes while using new observations to improve classes that were previously rare.

Dual-Balance Collaborative Experts addresses these two problems through different parts of its design. A group of experts specializes in classes with particular frequency levels, using tailored training losses. A dynamic selector then determines how to use these experts. The selector learns from synthetic features produced through balanced Gaussian sampling based on historical class statistics.

These synthetic features let the selection mechanism account for earlier class distributions when learning how to combine expertise. The intended balance is between preserving strong existing knowledge and improving weak historical knowledge with newly available data. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance, supporting this combined treatment of imbalance within domains and distribution changes across them.
icml-2025-addressing-imbalanced-domain-i.tldr: DCE combines frequency-specialized experts with a learned selector to handle class imbalance as domains change.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language question into SQL requires choosing a sequence of query-building decisions. Alpha-SQL tackles this task without task-specific fine-tuning, motivated by the expense and effort of repeatedly adapting newly released language models. Its central idea is to search through possible constructions instead of relying on a single generated query.

The method uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore SQL construction from partially completed reasoning states. A language model acts as an action generator, proposing possible next construction steps during the search. This makes the available actions responsive to the current reasoning state. A self-supervised reward function evaluates candidate queries and helps direct exploration toward promising alternatives.

On the BIRD development set, Alpha-SQL reports 69.7% execution accuracy using a 32-billion-parameter open-source model without fine-tuning. The abstract reports a 2.5% improvement over the best previous zero-shot approach based on GPT-4o. These findings support search guided by a language model as a useful way to improve query construction while avoiding task-specific model training.
icml-2025-alpha-sql-zero-shot-text-to-sq.tldr: Alpha-SQL uses language-model-guided tree search to build SQL queries without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Reward shaping helps reinforcement-learning agents learn faster by supplementing the feedback they receive. Choosing useful shaping signals often depends on manual design and domain knowledge. This paper develops an automated alternative that draws on previously collected data, including data that may be biased by unobserved factors affecting the recorded outcomes.

The method calculates causal upper bounds on state values from the offline dataset. These bounds provide optimistic estimates of how valuable states could be while accounting for possible confounding. The estimates become state potentials in potential-based reward shaping, providing the learner with an additional signal derived from the offline evidence.

The theoretical result applies when this shaping function is used with a model-free learner based on upper-confidence-bound principles. In that setting, the authors establish a better gap-dependent regret bound than for the learner without shaping. This concerns accumulated learning performance during online exploration. Simulations support the analysis, suggesting that appropriately constructed bounds can turn imperfect historical data into useful guidance for subsequent learning.
icml-2025-automatic-reward-shaping-from-.tldr: Causal value bounds from potentially confounded offline data provide automated reward shaping with improved regret guarantees for a specified learner.

paragraphs: An image edit can follow an instruction in one area while accidentally changing unrelated content elsewhere. Assessing editing quality therefore requires checking both the requested modification and the preservation of everything outside its scope. The paper introduces Balancing Preservation Modification, or BPM, to evaluate these two responsibilities explicitly.

BPM first locates the regions relevant to the instruction. Its Region-Aware Judge checks whether the location and size of the edited area fit the request. Its Semantic-Aware Judge then evaluates whether the relevant region contains the requested change and whether unrelated regions retain their content. Separating these judgments makes the assessment more interpretable than a score that combines all image changes indiscriminately.

Across the evaluated instruction-editing data, BPM achieves the strongest agreement with human evaluation among the compared metrics. The authors also show that its region-localization component can be incorporated into editing methods to improve their outputs. The contribution thus includes both a way to assess edits and a component that can help guide where changes should occur.
icml-2025-balancing-preservation-and-mod.tldr: BPM evaluates image edits by separately checking where changes occur, whether they follow instructions, and whether unrelated content is preserved.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model can change the data it later encounters. This creates a feedback loop between predictions and future outcomes. The paper studies clipped stochastic gradient descent in this setting, motivated by privacy-preserving optimization. Clipping complicates the updates, while changing data distributions mean the dynamics no longer behave like ordinary gradient optimization.

The authors characterize a stochastic bias introduced by clipping in projected clipped SGD. This bias prevents the algorithm from reaching a performatively stable solution. For strongly convex losses, they establish lower and upper bounds and show that greater sensitivity of the data distribution can amplify the bias. For nonconvex losses, they bound the remaining stationarity bias.

The paper then studies two remedies: an optimal step-size design for projected clipped SGD and the use of DiceSGD. Its extended analysis shows that DiceSGD avoids this stochastic bias in the performative setting. Numerical experiments support the findings, connecting the theoretical bias analysis to practical choices about which update rule and step sizes to use.
icml-2025-clipped-sgd-algorithms-for-per.tldr: The paper bounds clipping-induced bias when models influence future data and analyzes step-size choices and DiceSGD as remedies.

paragraphs: Long-context language-model inference requires storing a growing key-value cache, which can exhaust GPU memory. CommVQ compresses this cache through additive vector quantization. A lightweight encoder and a learned codebook represent cache contents compactly, while reconstruction can be performed using simple matrix multiplication.

The codebook is designed to commute with Rotary Position Embedding, the model's positional encoding operation. This compatibility lets decoding integrate efficiently into self-attention instead of adding a separate expensive reconstruction process. The authors train the codebook using an Expectation-Maximization algorithm. The design therefore addresses both storage reduction and the computational overhead of using compressed representations.

On long-context benchmarks and GSM8K, the reported 2-bit configuration reduces cache size by 87.5% relative to FP16 and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art quantization methods. The authors also report 1-bit cache quantization with minimal accuracy loss. This enables a LLaMA-3.1 8B model to use a 128K context on a single RTX 4090, illustrating how cache compression can make a demanding inference configuration fit available hardware.
icml-2025-commvq-commutative-vector-quan.tldr: CommVQ compresses the KV cache with a positional-encoding-compatible codebook, enabling low-bit storage with efficient attention integration.

paragraphs: A first-person camera records a wearer's surroundings, but that footage can also reveal information about the person wearing it. EgoPrivacy investigates this privacy exposure directly. The paper introduces a large-scale benchmark focused on recovering private information about camera wearers from their egocentric videos.

The benchmark covers demographic, individual, and situational privacy through seven tasks. These range from identifying a specific wearer to inferring broader attributes such as age group. The authors also introduce Retrieval-Augmented Attack, which uses retrieval from an external collection of third-person videos to strengthen demographic attacks. This examines how information outside the original first-person footage can increase the effectiveness of inference.

The evaluation compares attacks across the benchmark's threat models and finds substantial leakage of wearer information. The authors report that foundation models recover attributes including identity, scene, gender, and race with 70–80% accuracy even in zero-shot settings. These results show that the privacy implications of first-person recording extend to the wearer, including information that models can infer without task-specific training.
icml-2025-egoprivacy-what-your-first-per.tldr: EgoPrivacy benchmarks how first-person video can expose private information about its wearer, including through zero-shot foundation-model attacks.

paragraphs: Long-tailed classification involves many examples from common classes and few from rare ones, making generalization especially difficult for the rare classes. Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, seeks model parameters whose loss remains low under nearby perturbations. Existing adaptations for long-tailed data face a trade-off between computational expense and how precisely they control class-specific sharpness.

The paper contrasts two approaches: ImbSAM saves computation by excluding common classes from the SAM process, while CC-SAM uses class-dependent perturbations that require multiple backpropagations. Focal-SAM instead assigns different penalties to the sharpness associated with each class. This provides finer control without requiring extra backpropagations.

The authors also analyze generalization and derive a tighter bound for their method. Experiments with both traditional models and foundation models support its effectiveness. The contribution is a training objective that can treat classes differently while retaining computational efficiency, addressing the tension between giving rare classes appropriate attention and avoiding the cost of separately computing more elaborate updates for different classes.
icml-2025-focal-sam-focal-sharpness-awar.tldr: Focal-SAM applies class-specific sharpness penalties to improve long-tailed classification without extra backpropagations.

paragraphs: Generating a high-quality molecule is especially challenging when it must satisfy specified properties. GeoRCG divides this task into two stages. It first generates an informative geometric representation, then generates a molecule conditioned on that representation. The intermediate representation is easier to generate and provides structured guidance for the more demanding molecular generation step.

The framework comes with theoretical guarantees and is applied to EDM and SemlaFlow as base generators. Its central contribution is the use of semantically informative geometry as a conditioning signal. This gives the molecule generator a goal-oriented intermediate target rather than requiring the complete generation process to happen in one stage.

The authors report significant improvements in unconditional generation on QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, and an average 50% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches in conditional generation. Representation guidance also permits reducing diffusion from 1,000 steps to as few as 100 while largely preserving generation quality. These findings connect the intermediate representation to both better outputs and fewer generation iterations in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-geometric-representation-condi.tldr: GeoRCG generates a geometric representation before a molecule, improving reported generation quality and reducing required diffusion iterations.

paragraphs: Quantizing a transformer introduces approximation errors that can accumulate as information passes through its layers. GPTAQ addresses this accumulation without fine-tuning. During calibration, it matches each quantized layer's output to the corresponding output of the full-precision model, retaining an exact reference for what that layer should produce.

The authors call this asymmetric calibration. Their formulation accounts for both the current layer's quantization error and the mismatch inherited from earlier layers. Using optimal brain compression, they derive a closed-form solution for this combined problem. Channel parallelization, neuron decomposition, and a Cholesky-based reformulation make the calculation more efficient.

GPTAQ improves low-bit performance over GPTQ while requiring only about 20 additional lines of implementation code, according to the abstract. The authors also demonstrate quantization of a 405-billion-parameter language transformer and the EVA-02 vision transformer on a single GPU. Together, these results show the practical reach of correcting accumulated calibration errors while keeping the procedure lightweight enough for very large transformer architectures.
icml-2025-gptaq-efficient-finetuning-fre.tldr: GPTAQ calibrates quantized layers against full-precision outputs to reduce accumulated error without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up autoregressive generation by having a draft model propose several future tokens for a target language model to verify. Multi-head draft models assign different prediction heads to positions in that proposed sequence. Gumiho questions the practice of giving every position the same architecture and treating all draft tokens as equally important.

The authors theoretically establish that earlier tokens matter more than later ones. Their hybrid design allocates more computation to those early predictions: sophisticated Transformer heads operate serially at the beginning of the draft. Later positions use lightweight multilayer perceptron heads that operate in parallel, favoring efficiency where additional prediction effort is less valuable.

This allocation connects architectural complexity and execution time to a token's position in the draft sequence. It combines careful early prediction with inexpensive later proposals, rather than using a uniform generation pattern throughout. Experiments report better performance than existing approaches, supporting the idea that unequal computational investment across draft positions can improve speculative decoding overall.
icml-2025-gumiho-a-hybrid-architecture-t.tldr: Gumiho improves speculative decoding by using stronger serial heads for early tokens and lightweight parallel heads for later tokens.

paragraphs: Explaining a point-cloud model requires more than highlighting scattered points that appear important. A useful explanation should identify points that influence the prediction while also forming structures a person can recognize. InfoCons targets this combination by treating meaningful subsets of a three-dimensional point cloud as the concepts behind an explanation.

The framework uses information-theoretic principles to decompose an input point cloud into 3D concepts. With learnable priors, it examines how these concepts causally affect model predictions. The goal is to connect predictive importance with conceptual coherence, allowing a person investigating a failure to reason about recognizable structures instead of an unorganized collection of influential points.

The authors evaluate InfoCons qualitatively and quantitatively on synthetic classification datasets against four baselines. They also demonstrate scalability and flexibility on two real-world datasets and in two applications that use point-cloud critical scores. These evaluations examine both the explanatory framework and its usefulness beyond the initial synthetic setting, aligning with the paper's motivation of making model failures easier to diagnose.
icml-2025-infocons-identifying-interpret.tldr: InfoCons explains point-cloud predictions through meaningful 3D subsets that connect conceptual structure with predictive influence.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model's key-value cache can improve inference efficiency, but different transformer layers respond differently to quantization. KVTuner investigates this variation through the relationship between attention patterns and quantization error. It also examines why preserving key-cache precision is generally more important than preserving value-cache precision for reducing error.

The framework searches offline for hardware-friendly pairs of key and value precisions for each layer, balancing multiple objectives. Those configurations are then used directly during inference, avoiding repeated online precision decisions. To reduce calibration cost, the search prunes candidate precision pairs within layers and clusters layers to shrink the overall search space.

On mathematical reasoning tasks, the authors report nearly lossless mixed-precision caches averaging 3.25 bits for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 4.0 bits for the more sensitive Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The maximum reported throughput improvement over KIVI-KV8 is 21.25% across the evaluated context lengths. These results illustrate how allocating precision according to layer sensitivity can preserve task performance while improving inference efficiency.
icml-2025-kvtuner-sensitivity-aware-laye.tldr: KVTuner searches offline for layer-specific KV-cache precisions that improve inference efficiency while nearly preserving evaluated reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Pathology segmentation must distinguish tissue or cell regions in images where some categories are much rarer than others. L-Diffusion addresses the difficulty of learning useful features in this long-tailed setting. Its key modeling choice is to use multiple Laplace distributions, rather than Gaussian distributions, to represent distinct components in feature space.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting improved feature decomposition with this choice. Diffusion steps first produce a sequence of feature maps. Contrastive learning then refines the pixel-level vectors derived from that sequence, and the segmentation module uses these discriminative vectors to assign regions. The approach connects distribution modeling to the features used for individual pixel decisions.

Experiments report improvements on both tissue and cell segmentation datasets. For tissue segmentation, gains reach 7.16% in DICE and 16.52% in mIoU; for cell segmentation, they reach 20.09% and 14.42%, respectively. The abstract also reports improvements in MPA and FwIoU. These findings support the proposed feature-learning pipeline for segmentation, with the stated gains representing maxima in the evaluations.
icml-2025-l-diffusion-laplace-diffusion-.tldr: L-Diffusion combines Laplace-based feature modeling with contrastive learning to improve reported tissue and cell segmentation performance.

paragraphs: As language models accept longer inputs, practitioners face a choice about how to supply external information: retrieve selected material or use a long-context model. Existing comparisons have left this choice unsettled, in part because their benchmarks provide limited evidence. LaRA introduces a benchmark designed to examine the decision across a broader set of conditions.

The benchmark contains 2,326 test cases spanning four question-answering tasks and three types of long context. The authors analyze eleven language models using this evaluation. This structure allows the comparison to consider differences among models, tasks, and context settings instead of treating retrieval and long-context processing as two options with a single fixed ranking.

The main finding is that the better choice depends jointly on model capabilities, context length, task type, and retrieval characteristics. The study offers practical guidelines based on those interactions. Its significance is the conditional nature of the result: larger context windows alone do not settle which approach is preferable, and the choice needs to reflect the particular information-processing task.
icml-2025-lara-benchmarking-retrieval-au.tldr: LaRA finds that choosing between retrieval and long-context processing depends on the model, task, context length, and retrieval characteristics.

paragraphs: Embodied agents need to choose actions over long sequences, often before useful feedback becomes available. LARM aims to combine the deployment efficiency associated with reinforcement-learning agents and the generalization associated with large language models. It builds an action-producing agent from a language model with fewer than five billion parameters.

LARM directly predicts the next action to execute. During training, a much larger language model serves as a referee. The authors mathematically analyze how conventional reinforcement-learning feedback vanishes during long-horizon embodied exploration, and introduce referee reinforcement learning to address this problem. This places the large model's evaluative capability within the training process for the smaller acting model.

The resulting agent learns diverse open-world tasks without human intervention. A highlighted achievement is obtaining enchanted diamond equipment in Minecraft, which the authors describe as requiring substantially longer decision chains than prior leading achievements. This result supports the approach's ability to sustain progress across extended action sequences, where useful training feedback is particularly difficult to obtain.
icml-2025-larm-large-auto-regressive-mod.tldr: LARM uses a large-language-model referee during reinforcement learning to train a smaller action model for long-horizon embodied tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize classes without task-specific training, making them promising sources of weak supervision. However, converting their knowledge into accurate training labels remains challenging. This paper proposes a different labeling format: randomly and uniformly choose one candidate class, then ask whether an instance belongs to that class.

The resulting true-false label records membership in the sampled class rather than supplying a complete class assignment. The authors argue that vision-language models can generate these labels with high accuracy. They derive a risk-consistent estimator that uses the conditional probability information contained in this supervision, giving the learning method a theoretical foundation tied to the proposed labeling process.

The paper also introduces a convolution-based multi-modal prompt retrieval method to connect pretrained vision-language knowledge with the target task. Experiments support both the true-false labeling setting and the retrieval-based learning method. Together, the contributions show a way to use a simpler supervision question while still extracting information needed for the broader classification problem.
icml-2025-learning-from-true-false-label.tldr: The paper learns from vision-language-model-generated true-false class labels using a risk-consistent estimator and multi-modal prompt retrieval.

paragraphs: Agents trained with varied teammates need to learn differences that matter for coordination. SemDiv targets diversity expressed as meaningful behaviors, addressing the lack of semantic information in approaches based on randomization or policy-level diversity alone. It uses a language model to propose and describe new ways a teammate could coordinate.

Each iteration translates a natural-language behavior into a reward function and trains a teammate policy from it. Before using that teammate, the framework checks whether its policy is meaningful, novel, and consistent with the description. Agents then learn coordination policies for these teammates. Language-based reasoning helps select suitable specialized policies when an unfamiliar teammate appears.

Experiments show coverage of a broad range of coordination behaviors, including behaviors the evaluated baselines did not reach. Tests span four multi-agent reinforcement-learning environments, each with five unseen representative teammates, and report superior coordination and adaptability. The results support connecting teammate generation, behavioral verification, and policy selection through explicit language descriptions of coordination.
icml-2025-llm-assisted-semantically-dive.tldr: SemDiv generates teammates from language-described behaviors and uses that semantic structure to improve coordination with unfamiliar partners.

paragraphs: Selecting pretraining data for mathematical reasoning requires attention to the skills represented in that data. MASS builds this domain structure into selection through a graph of mathematical skills and their relationships. The graph is constructed from a reference dataset and provides the basis for evaluating examples in a target dataset.

MASS assigns quality scores using the skill graph, selects the highest-ranked subset, and uses that subset for language-model pretraining. Its contribution is a selection criterion informed by mathematical content and reasoning relationships. The authors evaluate the framework with one-billion- and seven-billion-parameter models, using both web-derived and synthetic pretraining data.

The results distinguish two benefits. With selected subsets, models reach similar performance to training on the original datasets while using 50–70% fewer training tokens. When the token budget is held equal, models trained on MASS-selected data perform 3.3–5.9% better. These findings suggest that skill-informed selection can improve either training efficiency or performance at a fixed training volume in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-mass-mathematical-data-selecti.tldr: MASS selects mathematical pretraining data using a skill graph, improving reported performance or reducing the tokens needed for comparable results.

paragraphs: Fourier Neural Operators offer a way to solve complex partial differential equations, but increasing their number of Fourier modes substantially increases parameter count. This makes tuning large models expensive. The paper asks whether settings found on smaller operators can be reused directly as the number of modes grows.

The proposed method, μTransfer-FNO, builds on Maximal Update Parametrization. The authors mathematically derive a parametrization designed to support the transfer of optimal hyperparameters between Fourier Neural Operators with different numbers of modes. This allows configurations tuned on smaller models to be applied to billion-parameter operators without another tuning stage.

Experiments across multiple partial differential equations validate the transfer approach. The empirical study reports lower computational costs for hyperparameter tuning while maintaining or improving accuracy on large models. The practical contribution is to make small-model tuning informative for substantially larger operators. It specifically addresses the scaling challenge created by adding Fourier modes, connecting the mathematical parametrization to a reduction in costly large-model experimentation.
icml-2025-maximal-update-parametrization.tldr: μTransfer-FNO transfers hyperparameters from small Fourier Neural Operators to much larger ones without additional tuning.

paragraphs: Removing an unwanted concept from a text-to-image model requires suppressing that concept while preserving useful generation of benign content. The paper attributes difficulties with text-only erasure to a gap between verbal descriptions and the visual knowledge involved in image generation. A prompt may not fully convey the visual features that need to be suppressed.

Co-Erasing therefore describes a target concept using both text prompts and the unwanted images those prompts produce. It applies negative guidance to reduce the probability of generating the target concept. A text-guided refinement strategy focuses the visual supervision on features most relevant to the named concept, aiming to avoid disrupting unrelated benign features.

The experiments suggest that this combined supervision significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art erasure methods in the balance between erasure effectiveness and continued usability. The approach matters because it addresses both sides of concept removal through the same visual evidence: identifying what should be suppressed and narrowing that suppression to the features associated with the specified concept.
icml-2025-one-image-is-worth-a-thousand-.tldr: Co-Erasing combines text and visual supervision to suppress unwanted image concepts while better preserving benign generation.

paragraphs: A language model can explain a solution in words while generating a program that follows different logic. The paper calls this mismatch a reasoning hallucination. Reasoning-as-Logic-Units, or RaLU, addresses the problem by checking the relationship between program operations and their natural-language explanations during inference.

RaLU begins with a generated program and uses static analysis to divide it into discrete logical units. It then conducts an iterative dialogue with the model to assess, refine, and explain each unit. A rewind-and-correct mechanism revisits statements to align them with task requirements. The final reasoning path follows the program's logic, with explanations attached to its individual units.

Experiments report significant improvements over existing baselines on mathematical reasoning tasks GSM8K and MATH, and algorithmic reasoning tasks HumanEval+ and MBPP+. These results support spending additional inference effort on local alignment between code and explanations. The method's interpretability contribution is to organize the solution around inspectable program units, making the connection between stated reasoning and implemented operations more explicit.
icml-2025-reasoning-as-logic-units-scali.tldr: RaLU improves reasoning by iteratively aligning small program units with their explanations and the task requirements.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning adds new classes over time while trying to retain knowledge of earlier ones. Replay methods support this by storing old examples and revisiting them, but those examples consume memory. Compressing the stored images can help, although the paper argues that existing pixel-level compression approaches offer an imperfect trade-off.

The proposed method uses tensor decomposition to exploit correlations among image pixels and the images' low intrinsic dimensionality. This produces compact representations while preserving enough discriminative information to support learning. The authors also introduce a hybrid exemplar-selection strategy intended to improve both how representative the stored examples are and how much diversity they cover.

Experiments across datasets with different image resolutions report substantial improvements to baseline methods, along with strong generalization and robustness. The approach combines two decisions that jointly determine the value of a replay memory: which examples to retain and how to represent them compactly. Its reported benefit comes from preserving useful learning information within compressed examples while improving the composition of the stored collection.
icml-2025-tensor-decomposition-based-mem.tldr: Tensor decomposition and hybrid exemplar selection make replay memory more efficient for learning new classes while retaining earlier knowledge.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization seeks parameters that perform well even at the highest-loss point in a nearby neighborhood. This can favor flat regions of the loss landscape, but its worst-case optimization is difficult in highly nonconvex problems. The paper also questions whether focusing exclusively on the single worst local outcome makes the best use of nearby information.

Tilted SAM replaces that focus with a smoothed objective based on exponential tilting. Nearby solutions with higher losses receive greater priority, controlled by a tilt parameter. As that parameter approaches infinity, the objective reduces to SAM. The authors show that the tilted objective is smoother, easier to optimize, and explicitly favors flatter minima.

They develop optimization algorithms motivated by discretized Hamiltonian dynamics. Across the evaluated image and text tasks, TSAM reaches flatter local minima and achieves better test performance than SAM and empirical risk minimization. These findings support a graded emphasis on high-loss neighboring solutions as a useful alternative to optimizing only the local worst case.
icml-2025-tilted-sharpness-aware-minimiz.tldr: Tilted SAM smooths sharpness-aware optimization by weighting nearby high-loss solutions, improving reported test performance across image and text tasks.

paragraphs: Implicit bias concerns the kinds of solutions that training tends to favor, and it is one proposed explanation for neural-network generalization. This paper studies that preference through the model's predictions over input space. It counts connected regions in which the predicted label stays the same, using this count to characterize nonlinear learned functions.

Unlike parameter norms or normalized margins, region count depends on the function the network computes. Changing the parameter representation without changing the function leaves the count unchanged. The authors argue that this makes the measure better suited to nonlinear, overparameterized models, where parameter-based descriptions may not directly capture the structure of the resulting predictions.

Empirically, smaller region counts align with simpler decision boundaries and correlate with better generalization. The authors also observe smaller counts with favorable hyperparameter choices, including larger learning rates and smaller batches. Their theoretical analysis connects learning rate to region count and explains how larger rates can reduce it. The findings provide a geometric account of training preferences while retaining the empirical distinction between correlation and guaranteed generalization.
icml-2025-understanding-nonlinear-implic.tldr: Counting connected prediction regions offers a function-based measure of implicit bias that correlates with simpler boundaries and better generalization.
